newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ bills close weaker, bonds retain firm tone.
newsitem.headline: NZ bills close weaker, bonds retain firm tone.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close

* NZ bank bills weaken as TWI falls, MCI loosens
* Mid-curve remains well bid
* Little material impact seen from RBNZ's new approach to
assessing monetary conditions
* Inflation-indexed bonds well sought after at tender
New Zealand bill rates closed higher on Thursday as the currency's Trade-Weighted Index shed 25 points, but the bond market remained well bid in hefty trade.
"The market hasn't moved very far, but there's been some good volume going through," said a senior bond dealer.
Bond yields ended a couple of points lower across the curve.

Dealers said slightly stronger-than-expected private sector wages data had been mildly felt in the money market, where the 90-day bank bill rate rose to 7.0 percent from 6.89 percent prior to the data's release.

Statistics New Zealand said average ordinary time private sector earnings rose 1.1 percent in the February quarter and 3.6 percent in the February year. Market expectations had been for rises in the order of 0.9 percent and 3.5 percent respectively.

But a debt market rate set this morning temporarily pushed the 90-day rate lower, dealers said, and the falling TWI also considerably loosened monetary conditions, with the Monetary Conditions Index (MCI) falling into the negative 90s.
Dealers said despite the easier conditions, short term rates were unlikely to move much higher with the RBNZ's June 27 Monetary Policy Statement (MPS) only three weeks away.
"I still feel there's reasonable scope for downside, particularly coming into the MPS at the end of the month," said a bill trader.

"Even with the potential easing signal yet to come, and the limited downside as a result of that, I think the market is probably going to cover any remaining short positions they may have out there, particularly in the bond market.
"For the Reserve Bank to come out now (to request a tightening of conditions), this close to the MPS, I think people are taking a bit of a gamble and assuming that they're not going to," he said.
The tender of NZ$50 million of inflation-indexed February 2016 bonds, which yielded 5.19 percent, attracted keen investing interest with bids totalling $172 million.
"I wouldn't mind betting most of that's gone offshore," a dealer said.
"They're not going to perform well at the moment, they're going to perform well at the end of the year when growth starts picking up."
The bond market was expected to hold around current levels going into key U.S. non-farm payrolls data on Friday night (NZT).

Meanwhile, the announcement of the Reserve Bank's decision to change its approach to assessing monetary conditions, while coming as something of a surprise, had little material impact on debt markets, dealers said.
The RBNZ said it would no longer assume nominal interest rates and the exchange rate to be constant in its June MPS.
Forex and debt market dealers said while the issue was technical and complex, a certain amount had been taken from the statement suggesting there might be more room to ease in future.
-- Matthew Brockett, Wellington Newsroom (64 4) 473-3736
